extraction.name: CommonsenseQA
extraction.description: A challenging new dataset for commonsense question answering containing 12,247 multiple-choice questions. Questions are generated by crowd workers who observe source and target concepts from ConceptNet and author questions that require commonsense knowledge to discriminate between semantically similar answer concepts. Each question has five candidate answers (one correct, four distractors).
extraction.creator: Alon Talmor, Jonathan Herzig, Nicholas Lourie, Jonathan Berant
extraction.publisher: Tel-Aviv University and Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence
extraction.citeAs: Talmor, A., Herzig, J., Lourie, N., & Berant, J. (2019). CommonsenseQA: A Question Answering Challenge Targeting Commonsense Knowledge. arXiv:1811.00937v2 [cs.CL].
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Subgraphs were extracted from ConceptNet, each with one source concept and three target concepts connected by the same relation. Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers were asked to author three questions per subgraph (one per target concept), add two additional distractors per question, and verify question quality. Web snippets were also collected via Google search for each question and candidate answer pair.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Web API, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The verification process filters out 15% of the questions that were not verified as answerable or correctly answered by at least one verifier.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: ConceptNet knowledge base (Speer et al., 2017), containing 32 million triplets. After filtering, 236,208 triplets were used, yielding approximately 130,000 triplets (43,000 question sets) for potential question generation. Web snippets were retrieved from Google search results (first 100 snippets per candidate answer, 500 snippets per question).
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: ConceptNet triplets were filtered by: (1) removing general relations (e.g., RelatedTo) or well-explored NLP relations (e.g., IsA), retaining 22 relations; (2) removing triplets where a concept is more than four words or not in English; (3) removing triplets where the edit distance between source and target concepts is too low. Question sets were formed by grouping three triplets sharing the same question concept and relation. The data was split into training/development/test sets with an 80/10/10 split, using either random split or question concept split.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Triplets from ConceptNet were filtered using three rules: removing general or well-explored relations, removing concepts longer than four words or not in English, and removing triplets with low edit distance between concepts. This resulted in 236,208 triplets. Questions were verified by a disjoint group of workers; only questions verified as answerable and correctly answered by at least one of two verifiers were retained, filtering out 15% of questions. Overall, 12,247 final examples were collected from 16,242 formulated questions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Amazon Mechanical Turk workers performed two roles: (1) Question authors: given a question concept and three answer concepts from ConceptNet, workers authored three questions (one per target concept) such that only the target concept is the correct answer. Workers were instructed to avoid surface clues strongly related to the answer. Workers also added two distractors per question: one selected from ConceptNet concepts with the same relation to the question concept, and one authored manually. (2) Verifiers: a disjoint group of workers annotated each question as unanswerable or chose the correct answer. Each question was verified by 2 workers; only questions correctly answered by at least one verifier were retained. For human evaluation, 100 random questions were answered by 5 workers not involved in question generation, with majority vote used for final accuracy.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Each question was verified by 2 workers. Questions were retained only if at least one verifier answered correctly, filtering out 15% of questions. Only annotators for which at least 75% of their formulated questions passed verification were accepted as question authors. For human evaluation, majority vote across 5 workers was used, yielding 88.9% accuracy.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 2 verifiers per question; 5 workers for human evaluation on a sample of 100 questions
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: 122 formulators contributed to question generation; 10 workers formulated more than 85% of the questions. Workers were Amazon Mechanical Turk workers. No further demographic information is provided.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: ConceptNet (Speer et al., 2017) was used for automated extraction of source/target concepts and distractor candidates. Google Search was used to automatically retrieve web snippets as textual context.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Dataset available for download at www.tau-nlp.org/commonsenseqa. Code for baselines available at github.com/jonathanherzig/commonsenseqa. No explicit versioning, update schedule, or deprecation policy is described.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance commonsense reasoning in NLU systems, which is a critical component for natural language understanding. By providing a benchmark that is easy for humans but hard for current models, it highlights the gap between human and machine commonsense understanding and encourages research into incorporating commonsense knowledge into NLU systems.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Questions were generated by a small number of workers (10 workers formulated more than 85% of the questions), which may introduce bias in question style and content. The dataset builds on ConceptNet, which may have its own coverage and cultural biases. Questions generated from AtLocation relation constitute 47.3% of the dataset, indicating an imbalance in relation types.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is based on ConceptNet, which may not cover all types of commonsense knowledge. Questions requiring reporting bias knowledge (information trivial to humans but seldom explicitly reported on the web) may be difficult for web-based models. The random split is harder for models that memorize question concept-answer associations. Web snippets retrieved via Google search do not appear to carry sufficient useful information for answering commonsense questions.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, development, and testing of commonsense question answering models. The dataset is split 80/10/10 for training/development/test. It can be used to evaluate NLU models on commonsense reasoning, including pre-trained models, fine-tuned models, and reading comprehension models using web snippets. Two split strategies are provided: random split (primary) and question concept split.
